story.title: Why I Built This Roadmap
story.subtitle: A note from Shea Bennett, founder of Shea's Tech
story.photoAlt: Shea Bennett, founder of Shea's Tech
body: Shea Bennett started his career in Information Technology as a Helpdesk Analyst with no formal training or background in IT. He had no experience when he left the U.S. Navy, where he served as a Hospital Corpsman assigned to a Marine Corps battalion as a Fleet Marine Force (FMF) combat medic. His dream was to become a medical doctor, but the cost of medical education was simply too high — not something the Montgomery GI Bill alone could cover.

While working as a surgical technologist passing instruments at Naval Medical Center San Diego, he met engineers from AGFA HealthCare and asked one of them for help getting into IT. To his surprise, the man helped him land his first real IT job. Shea then spent the next few years training onsite at AGFA HealthCare's headquarters in northern New Jersey, flying back and forth from San Diego. He struggled at first — he's a visual learner, and in 2007 the most common way to learn IT was in-person bootcamps or classroom training, neither of which he could afford.

Then he found Train Signal, video-based IT training, and never looked back. Shea is 100% self-taught. He went on to earn a Bachelor's and a Master's degree from National University in San Diego, and trained extensively alongside various government agencies and U.S. government IT contractors. He believes anyone can learn IT on their own without paying for a bootcamp — but that mentorship and networking, in person or on live video, are critical, because IT is a team sport.

He later married a Somali-Kenyan woman who opened his eyes to a world where most people can't afford the technology and training taken for granted in the U.S. and other wealthy countries — something he saw firsthand living and traveling in Kenya and beyond.

This roadmap is also an homage to his own start. When Shea got out of the Navy in San Diego with no money for anything beyond a cup of instant ramen from 7-Eleven, he had to focus on what mattered and hold onto every dollar just to make it. He eventually moved back home to Philadelphia, and after a year of real struggle, found a job in the DC Metro area — and never looked back.
quote: This was built for that fundi in Kenya, that hustler in Nigeria, the determined in Rwanda or Ethiopia. The hungry surviving in the UAE. The Indonesian or Filipino brother or sister — determined, but never given a chance or guidance.
It could be that street vendor in East London, West or North Philadelphia, the hoods of NJ, or in New York City. Or that front-desk hotel worker dreaming of changing their life.
story.closing: If anything here is wrong, report it and we'll fix it.

overview.title: How This Plan Works
overview.subtitle: Turning a job description into a week-by-week build schedule
body: This roadmap turns a real job description — designing, developing, and operating cloud-native applications on AWS — into a week-by-week study and build schedule. It is organized into 9 phases across 54 weeks at a sustainable pace of 8–10 hours/week. If you can commit 16–20 hours/week, run two plan-weeks per calendar week and finish in roughly 6–7 months.

Every phase pairs hands-on labs with a certification checkpoint, because the core asks — Linux, cloud infrastructure, CI/CD, IaC, containers, monitoring, security — map almost one-to-one onto the RHCSA and AWS certification tracks. Certifications aren't the goal; they're forcing functions that make sure you actually cover the breadth employers expect.

rhythm.text: hands-on labs and building (AWS Free Tier, a Linux lab machine, and a personal project repo)
review — write a short note on what you learned and what confused you

rows: Standard
~13 months (54 wks)
Follow the plan exactly: one plan-week per calendar week.
Accelerated
~6.5 months (27 wks)
Two consecutive plan-weeks per calendar week. Best if you're job-searching full time.
Extended
~16 months (68 wks)
Stretch each phase by ~25%; useful if you're working full-time with limited evenings.

note.title: A note on certification volume
note.text: Some working DevOps professionals recommend not over-indexing on certifications. If your goal is the fastest path to job-ready, treat Cloud Practitioner and Developer Associate as optional and spend the saved weeks on the capstone project plus Terraform and Kubernetes depth. Employers weigh a strong GitHub portfolio, the Professional-level cert, and demonstrable Linux skill most heavily.

stack.title: Linux First: Your Training Stack
stack.subtitle: Why Linux comes before AWS — and where to train it
body: Nearly every AWS workload in this plan runs on Linux: EC2 instances, container images, EKS worker nodes, build agents, and the shell you troubleshoot from. Engineers who skip this layer hit a wall around Phase 4, when a container won't start and the answer is a permissions bit, a systemd unit, or an SELinux label — not an AWS setting.
Phase 0 is therefore a full six-week Linux on-ramp, built around these resources.

resources.name: Learn Linux For Work
resources.desc: Structured, work-focused Linux training — the core curriculum for Phase 0. Start here before you touch the AWS phases.

resources.name: Doc Linux
resources.desc: The companion reference: command documentation and syntax lookups. Keep it open in a second tab while you lab.

resources.name: LinuxCert Guru
resources.desc: Hands-on RHCSA mock exams — timed, practical, performance-based. Your Week 4 checkpoint and recurring pressure test.

resources.name: Kubecraft Linux
resources.desc: Community classroom for Linux and Kubernetes — structured lessons plus people to ask when you get stuck.

resources.name: Red Hat Interactive Labs
resources.desc: Free browser-based RHEL labs from Red Hat. Zero setup, no VM required.

resources.name: LabEx
resources.desc: Guided live-environment labs for Linux, Docker, and Kubernetes.

resources.name: KodeKloud
resources.desc: Browser-based DevOps labs and playgrounds — Kubernetes, Terraform, Ansible, CI/CD.

resources.name: Linux Foundation
resources.desc: LFCS training and certification — the distro-neutral alternative to RHCSA.

note.title: Hands-on labs — the non-negotiable habit
note.text: Reading about Linux does not build Linux skill. Every week in Phase 0 ends with a lab you type yourself on a live system: break it, fix it, and write down what you did. Then prove it under time pressure with a mock exam. Can't finish a task without looking it up? Look it up, then redo the lab cold.

stack.outro: Browser labs are perfect for a quick repetition, but they reset when you close the tab. For the RHCSA you need a machine you own, can break, and can rebuild — that's the Home Lab section. Whatever you run on, keep a break/fix log in a Git repo from day one, and work in the terminal only — no GUI.

homelab.title: Build Your Home Lab
homelab.subtitle: Real hardware, real RHEL — the setup that actually prepares you for the RHCSA
body: The RHCSA is a hands-on exam — you are dropped at a shell prompt on a real Red Hat system and told to fix it. Browser labs are fine for reps, but they hide what bites you on exam day: bootloaders, partitioning, network config, and recovering a machine that won't boot. Install Linux on real hardware. A $120 used business laptop is the single best purchase in this plan.

startHere.title: Start here — the three-step path
steps: Buy a used business laptop (~$100–$200) with 16 GB RAM and an SSD.
Wipe it and install RHEL 10 using the free Red Hat Developer subscription (covers up to 16 machines), or Rocky Linux 10 if you'd rather not create an account.
Break it, fix it, reinstall it. Repeat until reinstalling is boring.

budgetNote.title: Don't buy everything at once
budgetNote.text: One used laptop running RHEL 10 gets you through Phase 0 and the RHCSA — that alone makes you job-ready on the Linux side. Add a home server around Phase 3 when Terraform and Kubernetes need more nodes, and networking gear only if you want CCNA-level practice. Everything in this section is optional except the first laptop.

groups.title: Pick your operating system
groups.intro: Both are RHEL 10 for exam purposes. Use real RHEL if you can; Rocky is the free rebuild — same commands, no account required.
columns: What it is and when to use it

items.name: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10
items.desc: The real thing. The Red Hat Developer Subscription for Individuals is free and covers up to 16 physical or virtual systems — more than enough for a full home lab. Create a free account, activate the subscription, then download the boot or DVD ISO (x86_64 or aarch64). Read the FAQ for the terms.

items.name: Rocky Linux 10
items.desc: A community rebuild of RHEL 10 — bug-for-bug compatible, no account, no limits. Use it for extra nodes once you've used up your 16 RHEL entitlements, or if you want to lab without registering anything.

after.title: Installing it
bullets: Download the DVD ISO from developers.redhat.com (RHEL) or rockylinux.org (Rocky).
Write it to a USB stick with dd or balenaEtcher, then boot the laptop from USB.
Install to bare metal — wipe the whole disk. This is a lab machine, not your daily driver.
Need more than one node? Install Oracle VirtualBox on a second machine (or on the laptop itself) and run 2–3 VMs. Snapshot before every lab so you can roll back in seconds.

groups.title: Used laptops (cheapest, recommended to start)
groups.intro: Off-lease corporate laptops are the best value in computing. Look for an Intel i5/i7 or Ryzen 5/7, 16 GB RAM, and a 256 GB+ SSD. ThinkPad T/X, Dell Latitude, and HP EliteBook all have excellent Linux driver support.

items.name: eBay — Renew4me
items.desc: Cleaned, tested, refurbished machines. Pay a little more, get something that works out of the box. Best first stop if this is your only lab machine.

items.name: eBay — NurTech
items.desc: Cheapest and roughest. Expect cosmetic damage and possible self-repairs (battery, keyboard, screen). Great value if you're comfortable with a screwdriver.

groups.title: Buy a new laptop built for Linux
groups.intro: If you'd rather not gamble on used hardware, these vendors ship Linux preinstalled and tested. More expensive, zero driver hunting.

groups.intro: Around Phase 3 one laptop stops being enough. Put a used server in a closet, run a free hypervisor, and you have a dozen VMs on demand.

certs.title: Certification Roadmap
certs.subtitle: One Linux cert, five AWS certs, taken in this order
body: RHCSA proves the Linux layer; the AWS track proves the cloud layer. Cloud Practitioner and Developer Associate are marked optional — include them if you want extra structure or are newer to IT, skip them to move faster toward the Professional-level cert.

note.title: Optional add-ons (post-plan)
note.text: AWS Certified Security – Specialty (SCS-C02) deepens the security and compliance bullet and is a strong differentiator for regulated or government-adjacent environments. On the Linux side, RHCE (EX294) is the natural follow-on to RHCSA and pairs directly with Phase 7's configuration management work; LFCS from the Linux Foundation is the distro-neutral alternative.

phases.title: Linux Foundations
phases.subtitle: Command line, systems administration, RHCSA readiness, Git, and scripting — before you touch AWS

tasks: Install RHEL 10 or Rocky Linux 10 on a real machine (see Home Lab)
Filesystem hierarchy, navigation, redirection, pipes, grep/sed/awk
File permissions, ownership, umask, ACLs; hard vs symbolic links
Lab: recover a system you locked yourself out of
Users, groups, sudo policy, password aging, /etc/skel
systemd: units, targets, systemctl, journald log analysis
Package management with dnf/yum, repos, and module streams
Scheduled tasks: cron, anacron, systemd timers
Partitions, LVM, filesystems, /etc/fstab, swap
NetworkManager/nmcli, static IPs, DNS, routing, firewalld
SELinux modes, contexts, booleans, and troubleshooting denials
TCP/IP and subnetting; curl, dig, traceroute, ss
Sit a full timed, hands-on RHCSA mock exam — no notes, no internet
Score it, log every missed objective, rebuild those labs from scratch
Repeat a second mock at the end of the week; target a clean pass
Optional: book the real EX200 for the end of Week 6
Branching, merging, rebasing, conflict resolution
Open a PR against a public repo; practice code review etiquette
Set up a GitHub org for the capstone project — start it now
Move your break/fix log into the repo and commit to it weekly
Bash: functions, arg parsing, set -euo pipefail, traps
Python: file I/O, error handling, venvs, requests
Write 3 automation scripts (log parser, backup script, API poller)
Install and configure boto3; make your first AWS API call

exit.title: Phase 0 exit criteria
exit.text: You can pass a timed RHCSA mock without notes, you push to Git without thinking about it, and you have three working automation scripts in a public repo. If any of those is shaky, spend an extra week here — every phase that follows assumes it.

phases.title: AWS Cloud Foundations
phases.subtitle: Core services, plus AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (optional but recommended)

tasks: Global infrastructure (regions/AZs), shared responsibility model
IAM: users, groups, roles, policies; enable MFA on root
Set up AWS Organizations plus a sandbox account with a budget alarm
Launch and connect to EC2 instances; AMIs and instance types
S3 buckets, storage classes, versioning; EBS vs EFS
Deploy a static site to S3 + CloudFront
Build a custom VPC: public/private subnets, route tables, IGW/NAT
Security groups vs NACLs; VPC peering basics
Diagram your VPC — keep it for your portfolio
RDS (Postgres/MySQL) setup, multi-AZ concept, snapshots
DynamoDB basics: partition keys, GSIs, on-demand vs provisioned
SQS and SNS: decouple two of your Week 6 scripts using a queue
The Well-Architected Framework's 6 pillars
Billing dashboards, Cost Explorer, budgets and alerts
Practice exam #1 for Cloud Practitioner; log your weak areas
Full practice exam(s); review every missed domain
Sit the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02) exam

phases.title: Architecture Deep Dive
phases.subtitle: Advanced AWS services, plus AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate

tasks: Auto Scaling Groups, launch templates, scaling policies
Application and Network Load Balancers, target groups, health checks
Transit Gateway, VPC peering at scale, Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect concepts
Route 53 routing policies and health checks
S3 lifecycle policies, replication, storage class analysis
FSx and Storage Gateway use cases — know when to pick what
Multi-AZ vs multi-region patterns; RTO/RPO tradeoffs
Design and diagram a DR strategy for a sample 3-tier app
KMS envelope encryption, Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store
IAM policy deep dive: conditions, permission boundaries, SCPs
Lambda (cold starts, concurrency, layers), API Gateway
Step Functions and EventBridge; build a small event-driven app
2–3 full-length SAA-C03 practice exams
Rebuild weak-area labs from scratch, untimed
Sit the AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate (SAA-C03) exam

phases.title: Infrastructure as Code
phases.subtitle: Terraform and CloudFormation, from syntax to a real provisioned environment

tasks: HCL syntax, providers, resources, variables, outputs
State file mechanics; local vs remote state
Modules, workspaces, remote state with S3 + DynamoDB locking
Refactor Week 9's hand-built VPC into a reusable Terraform module
Templates, parameters, stacks, change sets, nested stacks
Recreate one Terraform stack in CloudFormation to compare tradeoffs
AWS CDK overview (Python or TypeScript)
Write a one-pager: when to choose Terraform vs CloudFormation vs CDK
Provision a full multi-tier VPC + app infra (ALB, ASG, RDS) via Terraform
Push to GitHub with a README documenting the architecture
terraform validate/plan/fmt in a CI check
Static analysis with checkov or tflint; intro to policy-as-code (OPA/Sentinel)

phases.title: Containers & Kubernetes
phases.subtitle: Docker fundamentals through production-style Amazon EKS deployments

tasks: Images vs containers, Dockerfile best practices, multi-stage builds
Container networking and volumes; how namespaces and cgroups actually work
Docker Compose for multi-container apps
Push images to Amazon ECR; image scanning basics
Pods, Deployments, Services, Namespaces, ReplicaSets
kubectl fluency; run a local cluster with kind or minikube
Ingress controllers, ConfigMaps/Secrets, PersistentVolumes and Claims
Namespaces and RBAC basics
Stand up an EKS cluster (eksctl or Terraform)
IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA); node groups vs Fargate
Package your capstone app as a Helm chart
Set up ArgoCD or Flux for a GitOps deployment flow
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter
Pod disruption budgets, resource requests/limits, readiness/liveness probes
Deploy the containerized capstone app to EKS end-to-end
Document the deployment architecture in your repo

phases.title: CI/CD Pipelines
phases.subtitle: Pipeline design, plus AWS Certified Developer – Associate (optional)

tasks: Trunk-based development vs GitFlow; pipeline stages (build/test/deploy)
Testing pyramid: unit, integration, contract, smoke tests
CodePipeline + CodeBuild + CodeDeploy end-to-end for the capstone app
CodeArtifact for package and dependency management
Build a workflow: lint → test → build image → push to ECR → deploy to EKS
Optional: stand up Jenkins in a container to compare self-hosted vs managed CI
Blue/green and canary deployments on EKS and CodeDeploy
Feature flags and rollback procedures — practice triggering and rolling back a bad deploy
2 full-length DVA-C02 practice exams
Review Lambda, API Gateway, and CI/CD service limits and quirks
Sit the AWS Certified Developer – Associate (DVA-C02) exam, or skip it and bank the week for capstone work

phases.title: Monitoring & Observability
phases.subtitle: CloudWatch through open-source observability, plus AWS Certified SysOps Administrator – Associate

tasks: Metrics, custom metrics, log groups/insights, alarms, dashboards
Instrument the capstone app with X-Ray tracing
Deploy kube-prometheus-stack on your EKS cluster
Build a Grafana dashboard for the capstone app's key metrics
Ship container logs via Fluent Bit to OpenSearch or CloudWatch Logs
Practice log-based troubleshooting on an intentionally broken deploy
Write a runbook for your capstone app (common failure modes + remediation)
Learn SLOs/SLIs/error budgets; define one for the capstone app
2 full-length SOA-C02 practice exams
Review deployment, patching, and troubleshooting scenario questions
Sit the AWS Certified SysOps Administrator – Associate (SOA-C02) exam

phases.title: Security, Compliance & Agile Practice
phases.subtitle: Closing the security and collaboration gaps in the job description

tasks: Enable GuardDuty, Security Hub, and AWS Config with conformance packs
Set up Ansible for configuration management and patching on a small EC2 fleet — this is where your Phase 0 Linux work pays off directly
Review least-privilege IAM patterns across the whole capstone project
Harden a Linux host: SSH policy, firewalld, SELinux enforcing, CIS baseline
Learn Scrum ceremonies and Kanban; set up a Jira or GitHub Projects board
Write ADRs (architecture decision records) for 2–3 capstone decisions
Practice a mock design review or code review with a peer or mentor

phases.title: Capstone & Professional Certification
phases.subtitle: Pull every skill together into a portfolio project, then sit the Professional exam

tasks: Full stack: Terraform-provisioned VPC → EKS → containerized microservices → CI/CD → monitoring
Write a polished README with an architecture diagram and a short demo video/GIF
Publish the repo publicly — this is your interview artifact
Review all 6 exam domains: SDLC automation, config management/IaC, resilient solutions, monitoring/logging, incident response, security/compliance
3+ full-length DOP-C02 practice exams; redo any lab tied to a missed question
Sit the AWS Certified DevOps Engineer – Professional (DOP-C02) exam
Update your resume and LinkedIn with certs plus the capstone project link

Optional books (Terraform Up & Running, etc.)

note.title: The #1 cause of surprise AWS bills
note.text: Always shut down or destroy EKS clusters, RDS instances, and NAT gateways when you're not actively labbing. terraform destroy is your friend. Set a budget alarm in Week 7 and check Cost Explorer every Friday.

tips.title: Tips for Staying On Track
tips.subtitle: The habits that separate a finished plan from an abandoned one

items.head: Build in public.
items.text: Commit to the capstone repo weekly, even in small increments. It becomes your interview talking point and a public record of momentum.

items.head: Keep a break/fix log.
items.text: Every error you hit and how you solved it. Start it in Week 1 alongside your Linux labs. This is gold for interviews and for your own review.

items.head: Lab it, don't read it.
items.text: If you haven't typed it on a live system, you don't know it. Pair every reading session with a hands-on lab the same day — Red Hat Interactive Labs, LabEx, and KodeKloud all run in the browser.

items.head: Pressure-test with mocks.
items.text: Timed, hands-on mock exams expose the gaps that untimed practice hides. Redo any lab tied to a missed objective.

items.head: Don't chase 100% comprehension.
items.text: Associate-level material sticks better after professional-level review. Flag it, keep moving, revisit during the review week before each exam.

items.head: Find an accountability partner.
items.text: Especially for the DOP-C02 push in Weeks 51–54 — it's the hardest exam in the plan.

items.head: Buy the voucher early.
items.text: Treat every exam voucher purchase as a deadline. Buy it 2–3 weeks out to force commitment.

items.head: Revisit the fundamentals.
items.text: When a Kubernetes or AWS problem stops making sense, drop down a layer — it's usually Linux.
